title: A daughter is better
hook: the king is disappointed at a daughter; the Buddha says she may do better than a son (SN 3.16)

segments.voice: Yesterday: four mountains rolling in on King Pasenadi, and your line, what matters most. Today the same king gets news from home, and doesn't like it.

King Pasenadi is sitting with the Buddha when a man comes in and whispers in his ear. Queen Mallika has given birth. A daughter. And the text says it plainly: the king was displeased. It doesn't say why. Some readers point to a world where a son carried the throne and the family line. The Buddha sees the king's face, and answers it with one short verse, spoken to the king himself, right where he sits.
screen: `A WHISPER IN THE KING'S EAR.` → `A DAUGHTER, AND HE'S DISPLEASED.` → `THE BUDDHA SEES HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: SN 3.16 is just the scene and one verse. A woman, lord of the people, may turn out better than a man. She may be wise and virtuous. And her son may become a hero, a ruler of lands. That's the whole teaching, and it's worth being honest about both halves. The first half is bold for its setting. In a court where a girl's birth was met with a frown, the Buddha tells the king himself that a daughter may be better than a son. Better, not just as good. And he says why: wisdom and virtue, qualities of the person, not of the body. The second half speaks in the terms of its time. The verse praises her as a devoted wife who honors her husband's mother, and as the mother of a son who may rule. Those were roles the king would recognize, and the verse meets him there. Some modern readers notice that tension, and some Buddhist teachers discuss it openly. Still, the verse was spoken to change a father's face. The sutta doesn't tell us what the king said next. And Queen Mallika herself appears elsewhere in the texts as a thoughtful follower of the Buddha; tradition says she started life as the daughter of a garland-maker. A garland-maker's daughter who became a queen. The birth that disappointed a king is, in a way, her story too.
screen: `A WHISPER: IT'S A DAUGHTER` · `SHE MAY TURN OUT BETTER` · `WISE AND VIRTUOUS, IN HER OWN RIGHT` · `SPOKEN IN THE TERMS OF ITS TIME` · then, large: `A DAUGHTER MAY BE BETTER.`

segments.voice: Remember something that arrived in your life and wasn't what you wanted, a job, a move, a person you didn't expect to matter, and notice your first reaction, the frown, the way the king frowned. Now look at what that thing became; maybe it turned out better, maybe it's still unfolding. Either way, breathe, and let a little room open around it.
Mallika. Pasenadi's queen, the mother in SN 3.16 whose daughter's birth made the king frown, until the Buddha said a woman may turn out better than a man. Today's word.
Your line: a daughter may be better. Wisdom and virtue belong to the person, not the body. Day six hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers cite the verse to Pasenadi when discussing the place of women and girls, and some communities read it alongside the nuns' own verses in the Therigatha.

original.note: Pali Mallika: jasmine, and the name of Pasenadi's queen, the mother in SN 3.16.

trapdoor: what you thought: a daughter is better is a modern slogan.
what it means: in SN 3.16, the Buddha tells a disappointed king that a woman may turn out better than a man, wise and virtuous.

what a scholar hears: the verse's praise also uses the roles of its age, a wife who honors her mother-in-law and the mother of a ruler; some scholars read it as both bold for its court and bounded by its time.

chat.says: What did the Buddha say when a king frowned at having a daughter?
options: That a daughter may turn out better than a son: wise and virtuous.
That he should hope for a son next time, to carry on the throne.
That she'd only matter as the mother of some future king.
chat.meaning: In SN 3.16 the Buddha tells Pasenadi a woman may turn out better than a man, for wisdom and virtue, qualities of the person.

Pasenadi.meaning: the king of Kosala in the Buddha's time

Mallika.meaning: Pasenadi's queen, a follower of the Buddha

notes: SN 3.16 paraphrased. Confirm the scene (a man informs Pasenadi privately that Mallika has given birth to a daughter; the king is displeased) and the verse (a woman may be better than a male; wise, virtuous, devoted to her husband, revering her mother-in-law; her son may become a hero, a ruler of realms).
The reasons given for preferring sons in that society (throne, name, ancestral rites) are general historical background; please check or soften.
Mallika's origin as a garland-maker's daughter is from the commentaries (e.g. the Dhammapada commentary / Jataka); flagged as 'tradition says'.
'It seems to have been heard' is an inference; the sutta does not record the king's response after the verse. A Keeper may prefer to cut it.
The modern discussion of the verse's tension is presented without ranking; please confirm the framing is fair.
